title: Just listening
hook: kirtan is the singing of the Guru's hymns, and the first practice is simply to listen

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva, chosen small enough to keep. Your line was one seva, kept.

There's probably a song you've heard a hundred times and never actually listened to. It plays in the store, in the car, in the background of your life. Then one day you hear it with headphones, eyes closed, and catch the harmony underneath, a line you never noticed. It's a different song. Now go to the Golden Temple in Amritsar, before dawn. From the center of the pool, music is already drifting out across the water. Voices, a harmonium, a drum. It goes on almost all day, every day. People sit along the walkway with their eyes closed. Not singing. Not reading. Just listening.
screen: `THE SONG YOU NEVER HEARD.` → `AMRITSAR, BEFORE DAWN.` → `EYES CLOSED, JUST LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Kirtan. The singing of the Guru's hymns, the shabads of the Guru Granth Sahib, set to music. It's at the heart of Sikh worship. Think back to day thirty-one: Guru Nanak didn't write his hymns to be read silently. He sang them, with Mardana playing the rebab beside him. The Gurus were musicians. Most of the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by musical mood, which is tomorrow's word. So for Sikhs, the Word comes most fully alive when it's sung. Guru Arjan says it plainly, in paraphrase: in this dark age, kirtan, singing the praises of God, is the highest practice. There's a practical reason too. Music gets past the part of you that argues. You can resist an idea; it's harder to resist a melody. But camp three starts not with singing, with listening. The Japji, you'll remember, gives four whole stanzas to listening, and kirtan begins the same way. Before you learn a tune or a word, you let the sound in. You don't have to understand Gurmukhi, know the raga, or feel anything special. Just listen, the way you'd listen to a friend telling you something important. Sikhs say the sound itself does something: listening to gurbani with attention is already a kind of remembering. Over the coming days, you'll move from listening to singing. Today, it's only your ears.
screen: `KIRTAN — SINGING THE HYMNS.` · `THE GURUS WERE MUSICIANS.` · `IN THIS AGE, KIRTAN IS HIGHEST.` · `FIRST, ONLY YOUR EARS.` · then, large: `JUST LISTEN.`

segments.voice: If you can, play one shabad, any one; many gurdwaras stream their kirtan live, including the Golden Temple, and if you can't, simply listen to the room around you. Close your eyes, don't try to understand or hum along, and let the sound arrive: the voice, the drum, the pause between phrases. When your mind drifts, come back to the sound, as many times as it takes.
Kirtan. The singing of the Guru's hymns, and for camp three, the practice that begins with simply listening.
Your line: just listen. No phone, no dishes, just ears. Day one hundred four.

screen: `DAY 104 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOOD OF A RAGA.`

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, musicians called ragis sing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib while the congregation listens, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar kirtan continues for most of the day and is broadcast live.

chat.says: Do I need to understand Punjabi to get anything from kirtan?
options: No. Kirtan starts with just listening, and Sikhs say attentive listening is remembering.
Yes. Kirtan only means something once you can read the Gurmukhi script.
No, because kirtan is background music; you don't need to pay attention.

Ang 1075 (kalijug mahi kirtan pardhana) paraphrased; confirm Ang.

'Listening to gurbani with attention is already a kind of remembering': summary of gurmat teaching; confirm.
